newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-ROME AND ATHENS EMERGE AS FRONTRUNNERS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ROME AND ATHENS EMERGE AS FRONTRUNNERS.

text.p: Rome and Athens emerged from the International Olympic Committee's 350 page evaluation report on Thursday as front-runners in the race to host the 2004 Olympics.
Cape Town meanwhile, once touted as the early favourite, may have been robbed of its bid to stage the 28th Summer Games by its crimewave.
Although there was no clear favourite among the 11 candidates as there was in the fight to host the 2000 Games when Sydney was the bid to beat, Rome and Athens each received positive reviews.

Istanbul, Lille, St Petersburg, Stockholm, Seville, San Juan, Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires are the other cities battling for a place among the five finalists to be announced on March 7 in Lausanne.
The winner will be named on September 5.

Athens, which felt snubbed when the 1996 centenary Olympics were awarded to Atlanta and vowed never to bid for the Games again, has abandoned its view that the world owes it an Olympics and instead concentrated on convincing the IOC that it can do the job.
Once considered a harbour for terrorists, a city plagued by strikes, pollution and economic problems, Athens has worked hard to transform its image as a whiner to a that of a winner.

Pollution remains a major concern, a problem that could be compounded by the possibility of high temperatures (40 degrees Celsius) but the report noted that government efforts in the transport and energy sector had shown positive results.
While Athens's nightmarish traffic problems were also noted, there was no specific mention of security problems and terrorism, big concerns in its earlier bid.
The Athens bid also enjoyed the strongest local support of the 11 candidates, its four million citizens 96.4 percent in favour of staging the Games.
Stockholm, also considered among the contenders, has had its bid damaged by a poll that indicated only 32 percent of the population agreed with staging the Olympics while 52 percent were against.

That aside, the Stockholm bid received high marks in almost every other area. IOC inspectors were impressed by the many facilities already in place and the fact that 75 percent of the venues would be within walking distance. The report also noted there was plenty of adequate accommodation and an extensive and a reliable public transport system.
Aside from concerns about traffic, the evaluation report seemed to find no glaring weakness in Rome's bid.

The city, which hosted the 1960 Games, already has many first class facilities in place, including two complexes used in the the 1994 world swimming championships and an 85,000 seat stadium used for the 1987 Athletics world championships and 1990 World Cup.

Cape Town's bid appealed to the IOC's social conscience by underlining that staging the Olympic Games in South Africa would create new jobs and help unify South Africans in their post-Apartheid period.

But IOC inspectors also noted that while the people of Cape Town were not generally against hosting the Olympics, many thought the city's candidature was premature, indicating that other priorities should prevail.

By the far the IOC's biggest concern about the Cape Town bid was the city's serious crime problems. The evaluation commission acknowledged that plans and a detailed strategy had been developed to improve security but added that full implementation of these plans over the coming years would be a challenge.
